title: Four Pages from Dacca: Bose, the Envelope to Berlin, and the Word That Outlived Him
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Calcutta, the eldest of seven
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the first day of 1894 a son is born in Calcutta to Surendranath Bose, an accountant in the East India Railways who will later go into business, and to Amodini Devi. He is the eldest of seven children and the only boy. No plaque marks the house; the record gives the city and nothing finer. The second capital of the British empire is thick with law courts, printing presses and examination halls. Nothing in the municipal record separates this birth from the others entered that week.
suggested_refs: The birth of 1 January 1894; the Calcutta house itself is nowhere documented
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Bara Jagulia, the village behind the family
stops.date_confidence: attested as the ancestral village; no visit by Bose is recorded at any date
stops.campa: Some forty-five kilometres north of Calcutta, in the Haringhata country of Nadia district, stands the village the Bose family came from. Satyendra Nath's branch has been in the city a generation by the time he is born, and no source records him going back to Bara Jagulia as a grown man. The village survives in his biography as a line of provenance, a district and a village entered at the head of the account before the rest of it moves to Calcutta's schools.
suggested_refs: Bara Jagulia, Haringhata block, Nadia district, named as the ancestral home

stops.name: Goabagan, the New Indian School
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year is inferred from his age at starting school, not stated in any source
stops.campa: His schooling begins at five, at a school near the house. When the family moves to Goabagan in north Calcutta he is admitted to the New Indian School, where Bengali readers and an English syllabus share the same crowded room, the standard double education of a colonial childhood. The lanes here are printers' lanes. The examinations that will decide his future are set in English; the readers on the same desk are Bengali. Both languages are in the room from the beginning.
suggested_refs: The New Indian School at Goabagan, north Calcutta
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Hindu School, fifth in order of merit
stops.date_confidence: attested; the 1908 attempt lost to illness is from the Academy memoir
stops.campa: He sits the entrance examination at Hindu School in 1908 and chicken pox takes him out of it; he stays a further year and passes in 1909, fifth in order of merit. Hindu School stands in the College Street quarter among the bookstalls, a few minutes on foot from the university halls where the rest of his life will happen. Fifth is not first, and the record keeps the number honestly. At fifteen the prodigy is one bright boy among the thousands the examination system ranks and files every year.
suggested_refs: Hindu School, Calcutta, and the matriculation lists of 1909
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Presidency College, first in mixed mathematics
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At Presidency College he is taught by Jagadish Chandra Bose, Prafulla Chandra Ray and Sarada Prasanna Das. He stands first in the intermediate science examination of 1911 and first again in the BSc in mixed mathematics in 1913. In March 1912 Hermann Keyserling passes through Calcutta on his round-the-world tour and writes of the two Indias he has found there. The second India, the one in the laboratories, is at that moment eighteen years old and sitting examinations on College Street.
suggested_refs: The Presidency College examination lists, 1911 and 1913

stops.name: Calcutta, the marriage to Ushabati Ghosh
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Academy memoir, which names her father and her age; MacTutor gives 1915 and the name Ushabala, and is not followed here
stops.campa: In 1914, twenty years old and still in the postgraduate class, he marries Ushabati Ghosh, the only daughter of Jogindranath Ghosh, a well-known Calcutta physician. She is eleven. The arrangement is unremarkable for the class and the decade, and the house it happened in is not written down anywhere. The marriage outlasts Dacca, Paris, Berlin and Santiniketan. It ends only at his death sixty years later, when he leaves Ushabati, two sons and five daughters behind him in the same city.
suggested_refs: The 1914 marriage; the wedding venue within Calcutta is undocumented
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Rajabazar Science College, the record MSc
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ashutosh Mukherjee has built a science college at Rajabazar out of Bengali money, for Bengali students, inside a system that expected neither. Bose sits the MSc in mixed mathematics there in 1915 and sets a mark in the university's records that stands for years afterwards. He stays on as a research scholar in relativity, then from 1916 as a lecturer in the physics department. He has no doctorate. He will never take one, and the omission follows him to every appointment he ever holds.
suggested_refs: The Science College at Rajabazar, founded by Ashutosh Mukherjee
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Rajabazar, the relativity papers put into English
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Academy memoir's bibliography; Wikipedia dates the volume 1919, and the two are not reconciled here
stops.campa: With Meghnad Saha, working from the German and the French, Bose translates the original papers of Einstein and Minkowski, and the university publishes them in Calcutta as 'The Principle of Relativity' with a historical introduction by P. C. Mahalanobis. Bose does the paper on generalised relativity himself. In December 1917 Annie Besant presides over the Indian National Congress in this same city; the young lecturer turning Einstein into English belongs to the other half of the same awakening, the half that will not be political.
stops.quote: I do not know whether you still remember that somebody from Calcutta asked your permission to translate your papers on Relativity in English. You acceded to the request. The book has since been published. I was the one who translated your paper on Generalised Relativity.
stops.quote_source: S. N. Bose, letter to Albert Einstein, 4 June 1924, recalling the translation
suggested_refs: M. N. Saha and S. N. Bose, 'The Principle of Relativity', University of Calcutta, 1920
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

segments.name: Dacca: A Department Out of Nothing

stops.name: Curzon Hall, Dacca, Reader in physics
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The University of Dacca is two years old and its physics department is a plan on paper. Bose arrives as Reader and finds the post closer to an expedition than an appointment: order the apparatus, raise the laboratory, write out courses in thermodynamics and Maxwell's electromagnetism for students who have no textbook fitted to them. Dacca is a provincial university trying to become a real one, and it has hired, to make its physics credible, a man of twenty-seven with no doctorate and no European training.
suggested_refs: Curzon Hall and the first physics laboratories of the University of Dacca

stops.name: Dacca, Saha brings the literature
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Academy memoir; the month is the memoir's, given as around March 1924
stops.campa: Planck's derivation has been troubling Bose in the lecture room: it borrows from classical electrodynamics the very quantity the quantum is supposed to replace. Meghnad Saha, his old collaborator on the relativity volume, comes to Dacca in the spring and puts the recent papers in front of him, Einstein and Ehrenfest, Pauli, Compton, Debye. Bose then sets about thinking deeply, in the memoir's phrase, and spending sleepless nights on the radiation problem, until he sees that blackbody radiation can be treated as a gas of photons.
suggested_refs: Einstein and Ehrenfest 1923, Pauli 1923, and the Compton and Debye papers Saha brought to Dacca
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Dacca, the phase cells counted differently
stops.date_confidence: the paper is attested; the story that it began as an accidental miscount in a lecture is a later tradition, carried by Wikipedia and absent from the Academy memoir
stops.campa: He writes a paper of four pages deriving Planck's law on two assumptions only: that the elementary cell of phase space has the volume h cubed, and that light quanta are not merely alike but indistinguishable, so that two of them exchanged do not make a new arrangement to be counted. A tradition repeated ever since holds that the whole thing began as a slip in a lecture that came out right. The memoir describes no slip. It describes months of deliberate work on a derivation he could not accept as it stood.
stops.quote: You will see that I have tried to deduce the coefficient 8π ν2/c3 in Planck's Law independent of classical electrodynamics, only assuming that the ultimate elementary region in the phase-space has the content h3.
stops.quote_source: S. N. Bose, letter to Albert Einstein, 4 June 1924
suggested_refs: S. N. Bose, 'Planck's Law and the Hypothesis of Light Quanta', the English manuscript of 1924
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Dacca, the letter of 4 June 1924
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Philosophical Magazine rejection is attested but neither its timing nor its grounds are known
stops.campa: He has sent the paper to the Philosophical Magazine in London and heard nothing back for a long time. So he makes a duplicate, addresses it to Albert Einstein in Berlin, and asks a complete stranger at the far end of an empire to read four pages by a Reader in Dacca and say whether they are worth printing. He offers as his one credential the fact that he is the man who put the paper on generalised relativity into English. He has no other introduction to offer and does not pretend to one.
stops.quote: Though a complete stranger to you, I do not feel any hesitation in making such a request. Because we are all your pupils though profiting only by your teachings through your writings.
stops.quote_source: S. N. Bose, letter to Albert Einstein, 4 June 1924, written in English
suggested_refs: The letter of 4 June 1924 from Dacca to Berlin, with the manuscript enclosed
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Haberlandstrasse 5, Einstein translates it himself
stops.date_confidence: the translation is attested and falls between 4 June and 2 July 1924; the flat rather than the office is inferred from Einstein's Berlin address
stops.campa: The envelope from Dacca reaches Einstein's flat in Schoneberg some time in June. What the four pages contain is a way of counting light quanta that yields Planck's law without borrowing a single classical assumption. He translates the four pages from English into German with his own hand, a courtesy he extends to almost nobody, and attaches a note of his own recommending it. Between the fourth of June and the second of July an unknown reader in Bengal acquires the best translator in physics.
suggested_refs: Einstein's apartment at Haberlandstrasse 5, Berlin-Schoneberg
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Zeitschrift fur Physik, received on the second of July
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The paper reaches the journal on the second of July and appears as 'Plancks Gesetz und Lichtquantenhypothese' in volume 26, pages 178 to 181, under Bose's name alone. Einstein's translator's note is printed beneath the paper, and it runs to a single sentence. No other introduction is offered for the author, and none is asked for. From this point the derivation is not an unplaced manuscript out of a colonial university; it is a paper in the central journal of German physics.
stops.quote: Boses Ableitung der Planckschen Formel bedeutet meiner Meinung nach einen wichtigen Fortschritt.
stops.quote_source: Albert Einstein, translator's note to S. N. Bose, 'Plancks Gesetz und Lichtquantenhypothese', Zeitschrift fur Physik 26 (1924)
suggested_refs: Zeitschrift fur Physik 26 (1924), pp. 178-181, with Einstein's appended note
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Berlin, the method carried over to matter
stops.date_confidence: the papers of 1924 and 1925 are attested; the exact Prussian Academy session is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Einstein does not stop at translating. He applies the same counting to a gas of ordinary atoms and finds that below a certain temperature a finite fraction of them must fall together into the single lowest state, a condensation with no classical analogue whatever. He asks the journal to print his own papers alongside Bose's. The prediction then waits seventy-one years for an apparatus cold enough to test it, and is confirmed in 1995. The phrase that binds the two names to each other dates from these months.
suggested_refs: Einstein's 1924-25 quantum theory of the monatomic ideal gas, predicting the condensate

stops.name: Paris, seventeen Rue du Sommerard
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Academy memoir: he sails in early September and reaches Paris around mid-October 1924
stops.campa: Dacca grants him two years of study leave on the strength of what has happened in Berlin. He sails in September and reaches Paris about the middle of October, taking a room at seventeen Rue du Sommerard in the fifth arrondissement, a few streets from the Sorbonne. He is thirty and has never before left India. He enters the Latin Quarter of 1924 with a famous paper, no doctorate and inadequate French. The paper has arrived ahead of him; nothing else has.
suggested_refs: 17 Rue du Sommerard, Paris 5e, Bose's lodging of 1924-25
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: College de France, the introduction to Langevin
stops.date_confidence: the introduction is attested; the month is inferred from his mid-October arrival
stops.campa: The Sanskritist Sylvain Levi writes him a letter to Paul Langevin, professor titulaire at the College de France, and Langevin opens what can be opened. He sends Bose on with a note to Marie Curie, and with another to Maurice de Broglie, whose private laboratory does X-ray spectroscopy. The whole chain is one of introductions; nothing in Paris runs on the paper alone. Bose spends his first weeks learning how a European scientific city is entered, which is to say, by somebody else's hand.
suggested_refs: Paul Langevin's chair at the College de France, held from 1909
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Institut du Radium, the interview with Madame Curie
stops.date_confidence: the interview is attested by the Academy memoir; the laboratory as its venue is inferred, and the month follows Langevin's introduction
stops.campa: He asks Curie for a place in her laboratory and she answers that he should spend longer on his French first. He does not press it. The interview is the whole of the encounter: he never works under her, never learns radioactive technique from her, and the wish, in the memoir's phrase, remains unfulfilled. Later accounts promote this half hour into a year inside the Institut du Radium. What happened is that a Bengali physicist was received politely by the most famous woman in science and told to come back with better French.
suggested_refs: The Institut du Radium, rue Pierre et Marie Curie, Paris
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Paris, X-rays in Maurice de Broglie's laboratory
stops.date_confidence: the laboratory and the year are attested; the pin is the canonical Paris pin rather than the laboratory address
stops.campa: Where he does work is the private laboratory Maurice de Broglie keeps in Paris, under Alexandre Dauvillier, the chief assistant, on X-ray spectroscopy and crystallography. It is bench work, plates and goniometers, the experimental training an Indian theorist could not get at home, and he publishes little out of it. He is in the house of one de Broglie brother while the other, Louis, is defending in the same city the thesis that gives matter a wave. No source puts the two of them in a room together.
suggested_refs: The private X-ray laboratory of Maurice de Broglie and his assistant Alexandre Dauvillier
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Berlin, the letter of 8 October 1925
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: After about a year in Paris he moves to Berlin and writes to Einstein asking for an appointment. Einstein is away on his annual visit to Leyden. The letter waits on a desk in a city where Bose knows almost nobody, and the meeting the entire journey was arranged around does not happen in October at all. He fills the weeks with lectures and with German, and with the strange position of being, in Berlin, a name that everyone in the field has read and that nobody in it has seen.
suggested_refs: Bose's letter to Einstein of 8 October 1925, seeking an appointment
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Berlin, the meeting
stops.date_confidence: attested; the memoir places it several weeks after the letter of 8 October, on Einstein's return from Leyden, so the month is inferred
stops.campa: Einstein comes back from Leyden and receives him. He asks Bose how he arrived at the derivation, and whether the new statistics means something novel about the way quanta interact; the answers are not recorded. Then he writes a letter of introduction admitting Bose to the Berlin physics colloquium, the room where in April Werner Heisenberg will lecture on matrix mechanics and be walked home afterwards by the same host. Eighteen months after the envelope left Dacca, the correspondent and the author are in one room.
suggested_refs: Einstein's letter of introduction admitting Bose to the Berlin physics colloquium
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose
heisenberg.journey.json, Berlin colloquium stop of 28 April 1926

stops.name: Bombay, the passage home
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no ship, port or date of arrival is documented in any source located
stops.campa: The leave ends and he goes home. No manifest survives, no ticket, no date of landing; the standard route between the wars runs Marseille to Bombay and the reconstruction puts him on it. The crossing is real and undocumented, three weeks of open water between the two halves of a life. Everything on either side of this passage is attested and the passage itself is a hole, stated here as a hole. He lands in an India where his name is now printed in German.
suggested_refs: The interwar Marseille to Bombay steamship line, the usual route home
sources: General knowledge of interwar Europe-India shipping; no Bose-specific voyage record located

stops.name: Dacca, the chair goes to another man first
stops.date_confidence: attested: he returns in 1926 and is appointed in 1927, against accounts that give a single 1926 date for both
stops.campa: He returns in 1926. Einstein has written to Dacca recommending him for the professorship, surprised to have been asked at all, since he considers the work already sufficient warrant for the post. The university offers the chair to D. M. Bose, who declines it. Only then, in 1927, does it appoint Satyendra Nath Bose Professor of Physics and Head of Department. The story usually told is that Einstein's word made him professor. What the record shows is that letter, and a committee that went to its second choice.
suggested_refs: Einstein's letter of recommendation to the University of Dacca, 1926
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Madras, president of the physics section
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Academy memoir and Banglapedia; MacTutor's 1939 appears to be a slip of a decade and is not followed
stops.campa: The Indian Science Congress meets at Madras and Bose presides over the section of physics and mathematics. He is thirty-five. The Congress is the annual parliament of Indian science, a body of men trained in colonial colleges who intend to run a scientific establishment of their own, and it is putting at the head of its physics a man who published in Zeitschrift fur Physik out of a Dacca lecture room. Professional recognition reaches him at home about five years after it reached him in Berlin.
suggested_refs: The Madras session of the Indian Science Congress, 1929
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Calcutta, Tagore dedicates his one science book
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Rabindranath Tagore writes a book of popular science in Bengali, 'Visva-Parichay', the only one he ever writes, and dedicates it to Satyendra Nath Bose. The poet who has argued for thirty years that Bengal must think in its own language hands the argument to a physicist who lectures in that language and publishes in three others. Bose will spend much of his later life on precisely this problem: Bengali scientific prose, a science society, a journal, and a technical vocabulary that does not exist yet and has to be made.
suggested_refs: Rabindranath Tagore, 'Visva-Parichay' (1937), dedicated to S. N. Bose

stops.name: Delhi, general president of the Indian Science Congress
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Fifteen years after Madras he takes the general presidency of the whole Congress, at Delhi, in the last full year of the war. India is three years from independence and its scientific institutions are already rehearsing the state they expect to serve. Bose speaks as the most internationally known physicist the country has produced, and as a man who has spent twenty-three years in a provincial department raising laboratories on money that had to be argued for line by line.
suggested_refs: The Delhi session of the Indian Science Congress, 1944

stops.name: Dacca, the last year
stops.date_confidence: the deanship is attested as running until 1945; its starting year is not dated in any source consulted
stops.campa: He has been Dean of the Faculty of Science, and by 1945 has given about a quarter of a century to Dacca. Communal tension is rising in the city and a chair has fallen vacant in Calcutta. He leaves for good. Partition is still two years away and will eventually put an international border across the road between his two universities, so the departure is not yet an exile; everything that will make it one is already moving around him. The laboratories he built in 1921 stay where they are.
suggested_refs: The Faculty of Science at Dacca, which Bose served as Dean until 1945
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: University of Calcutta, the Khaira Professorship
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Academy memoir, Banglapedia and MacTutor; Wikipedia dates the move 1947 and names a different chair, a contradiction left open
stops.campa: B. B. Roy dies suddenly and the Khaira Professorship at Calcutta University falls vacant. Bose accepts it and comes back to the city of his schooling at fifty-one, to hold the chair until 1956 and then be made professor emeritus. Some accounts move the return to 1947 and hang it on Partition; the Academy memoir and the Bengali reference works put it in 1945, with a death and a vacancy behind it, which is how professorships ordinarily change hands.
suggested_refs: The Khaira Professorship of Physics, University of Calcutta, vacated by the death of B. B. Roy
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Calcutta, the border falls between two universities
stops.date_confidence: the Partition is attested; Bose's departure from Dacca precedes it by two years and is not caused by it
stops.campa: In August the province is cut in half. Dacca, where he taught for twenty-four years, is in another country by morning, and the Bengali Hindu professional class he belongs to moves west in millions. Bose has already gone, two years early and for other reasons. What Partition takes from him is not a post but a return: the department he raised out of nothing is now abroad, and the road between the two halves of his working life requires a passport and a visa.
suggested_refs: The 1947 partition of Bengal, which placed Dacca in East Pakistan

stops.name: New Delhi, nominated to the Council of States
stops.date_confidence: the 1952 start is attested; the end of the term is disputed, 1958 per the Academy memoir and 2 April 1960 per Wikipedia
stops.campa: The Republic is two years old and its constitution reserves seats in the upper house for people nominated out of science, letters and the arts. Bose takes one. He has been president of the National Institute of Sciences of India since 1949 and is by now a fixture of the new state's scientific apparatus, a man consulted about institutions rather than about photons. He sits in New Delhi as the physicist the Republic exhibits, which is a different job from the one at Dacca.
suggested_refs: Bose's nominated seat in the Rajya Sabha, taken in April 1952
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: New Delhi, the Padma Vibhushan
stops.date_confidence: the award is attested on the official Padma list; the Delhi ceremony and Bose's presence at it are inferred from standard practice
stops.campa: The Government of India names him to the Padma Vibhushan, the second of the civil honours. The award is on the official list; whether he travelled to the capital to take it is in no source consulted. Thirty years after a Reader in Dacca posted four pages to a stranger, a state that did not exist then is decorating him for it. He is sixty and still at work, on unified field theory, on crystallography, on the composition of gases coming out of the ground.
suggested_refs: The Padma Vibhushan list of 1954

stops.name: Bern, the meeting that does not happen
stops.date_confidence: the exchange, the intended Bern meeting and the destroyed manuscript are attested by the Academy memoir; the date given here is Einstein's death
stops.campa: Bose has been sending Einstein his papers on unified field theory since 1953, and Einstein has replied that he does not quite follow how the solution is to be used in physics, and has discussed it at length in a paper of his own. Bose writes a long answer and plans to put it in his hand at Bern, at the fiftieth anniversary of relativity that summer. Einstein dies in April. When the news reaches Calcutta, Bose tears up the only copy of the reply and throws it away.
suggested_refs: The Bern jubilee of 1955, fifty years after the special theory; Bose's destroyed reply
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Bakreshwar, helium out of the hot springs
stops.date_confidence: the work is attested; its years are not precisely dated in the sources consulted and 1958 stands as a marker inside the late period
stops.campa: In Birbhum district, where hot water comes out of the ground and pilgrims come to Shiva, Bose studies the gases the springs release and the possibility of drawing helium out of them. It is practical geochemistry, about as far from indistinguishable photons as work in physics goes. The man who once repaired Planck's law by counting differently is now counting trace gases bubbling off a Bengali hillside, and gives no sign of regarding the second as a descent from the first.
suggested_refs: The Bakreshwar hot springs of Birbhum, studied for their helium content

stops.name: Santiniketan, Vice-Chancellor of Visva-Bharati
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He takes the vice-chancellorship of the university Tagore founded in the open air at Santiniketan, and holds it two years. The low red buildings under the flat Birbhum sky are about as far from the Prussian Academy as Bengal is able to put a scholar. Bose moves between the poet's university and the physicist's academy without any visible friction. He is arguing, in the only way he ever argues anything, that Bengali will serve as an adequate language for both.
suggested_refs: Visva-Bharati University at Santiniketan, founded by Rabindranath Tagore

stops.name: Stockholm, four nominations and no prize
stops.date_confidence: attested; Banerjee's letter is dated 12 January 1956, with further nominations in 1959 and twice in 1962
stops.campa: Kedareswar Banerjee, head of physics at Allahabad, writes to the Nobel Committee in January 1956 putting Bose's name forward. Three more nominations follow, in 1959 and twice in 1962. The committee's evaluator, Oskar Klein, judges the work insufficient on its own for the prize. Meanwhile the statistics is taught to every undergraduate in the world, and the condensate Einstein drew out of it takes a Nobel of its own in 2001, awarded to three men for making in a trap what Bose made on paper.
stops.quote: (1). He (Bose) made very outstanding contributions to physics by developing the statistics known after his name as Bose statistics. In recent years this statistics is found to be of profound importance in the classifications of fundamental particles and has contributed immensely to the development of nuclear physics. (2). During the period from 1953 to date, he has made a number of highly interesting contributions of far-reaching consequences on the subject of Einstein's Unitary Field Theory.
stops.quote_source: Kedareswar Banerjee, University of Allahabad, letter to the Nobel Committee for Physics, 12 January 1956, printed in Rajinder Singh, 'India's Nobel Prize Nominators and Nominees' (Shaker, 2016), pp. 26-27
suggested_refs: The Nobel Committee nomination archive, 1956, 1959 and 1962; Oskar Klein's evaluation
sources: Rajinder Singh, 'India's Nobel Prize Nominators and Nominees' (2016)

stops.name: London, elected to the Royal Society
stops.date_confidence: attested; the election is in London and Bose is in India, no travel being recorded
stops.campa: The Royal Society elects him a Fellow. He is in India. The election happens in London, in the body that has been the metropolitan arbiter of scientific standing for three centuries, and it falls on a man who never took a doctorate and whose central paper was rejected, or mislaid, by a British journal thirty-four years before. The Philosophical Magazine's referee is on record nowhere at all. The paper he did not print is by now in every textbook of statistical mechanics.
suggested_refs: The 1958 election of S. N. Bose to the Fellowship of the Royal Society

stops.name: Calcutta, National Professor
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Academy memoir, which heads the period 1958-74, and by MacTutor; Wikipedia dates the appointment 1959
stops.campa: His term at Santiniketan ends and he comes back to the University of Calcutta and to nuclear physics. The same year the Government of India makes him National Professor, the highest place the country gives a scholar, renewed across three five-year terms that run until his death. It is the last of his appointments and it outlasts every other line on the record: sixteen years in which the title is simply attached to him and the work goes on in the same rooms.
suggested_refs: The National Professorship, held across three five-year terms from 1958
sources: INSA Biographical Memoir of S. N. Bose

stops.name: Calcutta, all the recognition he deserves
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the remark is undated in the sources consulted and is placed here in the late Calcutta years
stops.campa: Asked in old age about the prize he did not get, Bose gives the answer that every Bengali account of him repeats afterwards. He keeps a house full of students and a habit of talk, the science society, the journal, the vocabulary work, the springs at Bakreshwar, the unified field papers nobody quite follows. The absence of the medal is a subject for other people to raise. It becomes, in the national telling, the proof of the man: the one Indian entitled to a grievance who declined to hold one.
stops.quote: I have got all the recognition I deserve.
stops.quote_source: S. N. Bose on the Nobel Prize, quoted in Outlook India; seen only as cited secondhand, the original article being unreachable
suggested_refs: The Outlook India interview carrying the remark, cited but not directly reachable
sources: Wikipedia, 'Satyendra Nath Bose', Legacy section, citing Outlook India

stops.name: Calcutta, the fourth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Satyendra Nath Bose dies in Calcutta at eighty, in the city where he was born and schooled and where, after Dacca and Paris and Berlin and Santiniketan, he chose to finish. He leaves Ushabati, two sons and five daughters. The house or hospital is named in no source consulted. What is fixed is the city, and the distance from wherever he died to the lane in Goabagan where a boy of five was once walked to school, which is a little over two kilometres.
suggested_refs: The death of 4 February 1974; the residence or hospital is undocumented

stops.name: Nimtala Ghat, the rite not recorded
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source located names the cremation ground; Nimtala stands here as a representative ghat, not a documented one
stops.campa: No source found in this research names the ground where his body was burned. Calcutta's Bengali Hindu dead of that generation go most often to Nimtala or Keoratala on the Hooghly, and a man of his standing would have drawn colleagues and students to whichever the family chose. The pin sits at Nimtala as an instance of the custom rather than a fact. The gap is left open instead of closed: the most public scientist in Bengal has an unrecorded funeral.
suggested_refs: Nimtala and Keoratala burning ghats on the Hooghly, the city's principal cremation grounds
sources: General knowledge of Calcutta Hindu cremation custom; no Bose-specific record located

stops.name: Palais de la Decouverte, Paris, Dirac names them
stops.date_confidence: attested; notes on the lecture survive in the Dirac Papers at the National Archives
stops.campa: Lecturing in Paris on developments in atomic theory, Paul Dirac calls the particles that obey these statistics bosons. Bose is fifty-one and Dean of Science at Calcutta by then; he is not in the room and is not consulted. The naming is the ordinary way physics honours a person, by turning him into a lower-case noun that undergraduates use without suspecting there was a man. Half the particles in the universe are now named after a Bengali who never took a doctorate.
suggested_refs: Notes on Dirac's lecture 'Developments in Atomic Theory', Palais de la Decouverte, 6 December 1945, Dirac Papers BW83/2/257889
sources: Wikipedia, 'Boson', citing Farmelo, 'The Strangest Man', p. 331 n. 64

stops.name: Salt Lake, the centre that carries his name
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: By act of Parliament the Government of India establishes the S. N. Bose National Centre for Basic Sciences at Salt Lake, on the eastern edge of Calcutta, an autonomous institute for basic research carrying his name. Twelve years after his death the state builds the laboratory that the Reader at Dacca had to improvise for himself in 1921. It is the usual shape of national memory: the thing the man needed, provided afterwards, with his name over the door.
stops.quote: You don't know who he was? Half the particles in the universe obey him!
stops.quote_source: An unnamed physics professor to a student, quoted in 'Original Vision, Forgotten Hero', The Telegraph (Calcutta), 3 January 2012
suggested_refs: The S. N. Bose National Centre for Basic Sciences, Salt Lake, established 1986
sources: Wikipedia, 'S.N. Bose National Centre for Basic Sciences'

stops.name: Gurusaday Road, the bust in the museum garden
stops.date_confidence: the bust and the 1994 stamp are attested; the date given is the stamp's centenary year
stops.campa: A bust of Bose stands in the garden of the Birla Industrial and Technological Museum in Calcutta. In his centenary year the Post Office puts his face on a stamp. This is the register in which a country keeps a scientist: a head in bronze among the school parties, a rectangle of gum and paper, a research institute out at Salt Lake, and a word in the physics of every other country on earth that nobody outside India connects to a boy from Goabagan and his four pages.
suggested_refs: The bust at the Birla Industrial and Technological Museum; the 1994 Indian commemorative stamp

stops.name: Dacca, the ninety-eighth anniversary of a posting
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the commemoration; the pin is placed at Dacca, where the letter was written, the event itself having no location
stops.campa: On the fourth of June 2022 the anniversary marked worldwide is neither a birth nor a death but a posting: ninety-eight years since a Reader in Dacca put four pages in an envelope addressed to Berlin. The commemoration is a drawing on a search page, seen by more people in one day than have read the paper since it was printed. What is being remembered is the act rather than the result, the morning somebody with no standing decided to write to somebody who had all of it.
suggested_refs: The Google Doodle of 4 June 2022, marking the anniversary of Bose's letter to Einstein
